segments.text: AI operates differently than any other software we've used before.
While it can perform tasks that seem impossible for a computer, the reason it works isn't
a mystery.
It's simply built on a different logic than standard applications.
Most software, like the calculator on your phone, is built using line-by-line instructions.
A programmer writes out the exact steps the program must follow for every possible scenario.
This chart shows the core of that logic.
Rules
The most common type is an if-then-else statement, creating a rigid path for data.
If the password matches the record, then it opens the app.
Else, if it doesn't match, it triggers an error message.
Because these rules are fixed and written in advance, the software produces the exact
same result every time it's run.
AI doesn't work this way.
A programmer doesn't write a rule for every situation.
Instead, the model identifies and relies on patterns it gathered during a process called
training.
This shows the two stages behind every AI response.
First, the model learns.
During training, it processes enormous data into numerical patterns.
Then it builds an answer one word at a time using probability.
It calculates the most likely next word, adds it, and repeats the loop until complete.
It must learn the patterns first.
Then it uses those patterns to construct every response from scratch.
Imagine a robot following a recipe.
It executes every step as written to produce the exact same meal every time.
That's how normal software follows rules.
AI is like a chef with no cookbook.
By recognizing cooking patterns, the chef can create a dish they've never made before.
We can see this in how different programs handle the same request, like asking for
a PlayStation 5 game recommendation.
Normal software follows a fixed rule to retrieve a game from a preset list, giving the same
answer every time.
AI uses learned patterns to build a fresh response.
If you ask three times, it provides three different games, based on the probabilities
it learned.
Rules repeat a programmed response, while patterns allow the software to build a new one.
This reliance on patterns gives AI an advantage with messy information.
Normal software requires structured data, information neatly organized into the rows
and columns the program expects.
But real-world information is often unstructured, buried in an email, scribbled
on a receipt, or hidden in an audio recording.
This lesson started as a series of handwritten notes on a legal pad,
with lines crossed out and ideas moved around.
And AI was able to recognize the patterns in those messy notes
and organize them into a clean first draft.
As shown here, normal software is limited to specific fields and file types it was built
to handle.
AI is flexible, taking unstructured inputs, like a PDF or a photo, and transforming them
into a summary, table, or image.
You provide the mess, and AI makes sense of it.
This means the most important skill is picking the right tool for the job.
Use normal software for tasks that must be exact and consistent.
Reserve AI for open-ended tasks where writing a fixed rule is impossible.
While these pattern-based capabilities are powerful,
they also introduce a specific set of vulnerabilities.
Because AI relies on flexible patterns instead of strict rules,
it is much harder to control.
Even the researchers who build these models cannot fully predict or lock down
every possible output.
This identifies AI's kryptonite.
It can generate massive scams or create deepfakes.
It can also be confident but wrong, producing answers that sound correct even when false.
Ultimately, trained behavior is harder to inspect and secure than written rules.
To address this, developers use a two-part approach.
They teach AI to avoid harmful behavior during training and add guardrails,
filters that block harmful requests.
But guardrails aren't perfect.
They can block harmless information or misdangerous requests.
The foundation that allows AI to solve messy, complex problems
is the same foundation that makes it unpredictable.
Its greatest capabilities will always come with these inherent risks.
